name: Adam Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach adults at the evening college, accompany a community choir and clean up recordings for a small studio. I have a bachelor's in music and years of useful work behind me, though I still ask a singer before changing a chord; I use AI now and then for sorting old sheets after our accompanist checks a tool.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sana works at a pharmacy counter, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. The music pay is typical, we have about two months of expenses saved, and there are some other colleges and music jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the choir that a faster room booking is useful, but a singer still has to hear the next chord from a person. My adult keyboard class will carry on next term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI now and then for sorting old chord sheets after our accompanist shows me a tool. Sana's pharmacy counter pay and my college contract cover the mortgage, but we have only about two months of expenses saved, so I watch choir bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll get the evening college's next-term teaching hours in writing and keep the choir's two signed December dates. If both concerts pay, I'll put seventy from each fee into a reserve after the children's winter costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because a missed show would thin a small cushion. The college hours and Sana's pay still make the next mortgage payment feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the choir postponed a concert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One choir concert was postponed in April, and the college wage covered our bills until it was rebooked. I did not need the reserve, but the delay made me check every date twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you promise the children a trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sana and I would check the college dates before putting down a trip deposit. An unsigned concert cannot pay for our children's trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the college to put a number beside every paid hour it replaces with software. I would ask for a fixed fee for preparing keyboard parts, even if the booking emails become automatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Arrangements and recording cleanup bring about a quarter of my pay. I expect clients to stop buying some of those hours, and two months saved would not cover a long run of smaller invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare last term's paid preparation with the new course contract and ask the college for a written minimum. In the first year of this change, I'll trial an AI chord-checker on my own old score only after our accompanist shows it works, its licence permits reuse, and I verify each note by ear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real cut to my own pay. I want to try the tool on my score, but I will still ask for paid preparation. A chord checker can catch a note; it cannot pay for the hour the college removes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the checker trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not upload any pupil audio to the checker without written family consent. If the trial changes a chord I can hear is right, I'd stop and return to the original score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What preparation fee would you ask the college for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for two paid preparation hours per keyboard class. If the college refuses, I would keep the current term while asking a nearby college about an actually posted tutor role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the choir that full AGI by 2028 could write every arrangement we sell, so the college should give teachers a paid-hours plan now. I would still play the signed winter concerts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could arrange, clean recordings and prepare lessons better and cheaper than I can. Robots able to play hands-on parts arrive around 2031; my organ work may last longer, but losing preparation and edit pay would strain the mortgage before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total last year's college, studio and choir income and ask the college for its 2028 teaching plan. In the first year after 2028, if paid hours fall by a third, I'll apply for a posted adult-music tutor role at a nearby college only if my bachelor's qualifies, pickup fits, and written net pay after travel replaces the lost income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect part of the editing pay to go and fear the college may reduce teaching too. Two months saved is a short search, not a way to live with lower fees forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the other college hiring now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A college nearby advertised adult music work last year, but nothing is open now. I would ask about the next posting without telling Sana I have another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you call the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If teaching and choir fees both fall, I would ask the mortgage lender about a temporary plan before arrears. Sana and I would read the total added interest in writing before accepting it.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, I still need steady work; robot players around 2039 may reach the choir. Editing fees can fade before 2036, so I need stronger paid teaching hours rather than relying on studio cleanup.

By 2036 I'll aim for four months of expenses saved from spare paid teaching and choir fees after household bills; in the first year after AGI, I'll take a posted college teaching role only if a written net offer after travel covers our mortgage and school pickup and leaves my choir night free.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because even ten years does not protect next term's editing invoice. The course can help, but I will not borrow from the house reserve before a college accepts it.

transcript.text: How would you know the certificate is useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask both colleges whether they recognise the certificate before paying the application fee. If neither does, I would keep my current pupils and look for another course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave the evening college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave the evening class only after another college signs paid hours and the new timetable fits the children. A job interview may be useful, but I cannot pay the mortgage with it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because edits could go while the college is deciding its teaching hours. A written paid-hours plan, a real tutor opening that fits the children, and clear lender terms would let Sana and me budget with facts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a new college would let me keep the choir. The community choir pays a fee and gives me singers I know by name.

headlineQuote: The community choir pays a fee and gives me singers I know by name.
portrait: Adam is a **43-year-old** experienced keyboard teacher with a music bachelor's, evening college classes, choir work and studio edits.
He uses **AI occasionally**, with two months saved, typical pay, two children and a mortgage.
He expects **editing and preparation** fees to fall before robots reach live playing three years after AGI.
He tests **paid circles** and new tools only with proved results, written terms, paid places and family-compatible work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because edit fees may fall before the college confirms paid teaching hours.
whatWouldHelp: A **written college plan**, real family-compatible vacancy and full lender costs would help the household budget.
